item.title: What the Windsurf Sale Means for the AI Coding Ecosystem in 2026
item.description: The Windsurf sale to Cognition after a failed $3B OpenAI deal reshapes the AI coding ecosystem. Here is what happened, why it matters, and what comes next for developers.
item.content:encoded:
The Windsurf sale to Cognition in July 2025, following a failed $3 billion acquisition by OpenAI and a talent grab by Google DeepMind, marks the most dramatic consolidation event in the AI coding tools market. The deal reshapes a fragmented landscape into three dominant players — Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and the combined Devin/Windsurf platform — and signals that the era of standalone AI coding startups is giving way to platform-level competition.

The Windsurf Saga — A Timeline of the Year’s Most Dramatic AI Acquisition Story

The Windsurf story begins with Codeium, an AI coding startup founded by Varun Mohan and Douglas Chen. In early 2025, the company rebranded to Windsurf and quickly became one of the most talked-about tools in the AI-assisted development space. What followed over the next six months was a whirlwind of deal-making, regulatory friction, talent raids, and ultimately a strategic acquisition that changed the competitive landscape.

May 2025: OpenAI agreed to acquire Windsurf for $3 billion, as reported by Bloomberg. The deal was one of the largest private AI acquisitions at the time and signaled OpenAI’s serious push into developer tools. Windsurf had built a strong product with over 1 million claimed users and hundreds of thousands of daily active users, making it an attractive target for the AI giant looking to expand beyond chat and into code generation.

July 2025: The OpenAI deal fell through. According to The Verge, regulatory concerns and strategic disagreements caused the acquisition to collapse. Within days, Google made its move — not to buy Windsurf, but to hire its key talent. CEO Varun Mohan, co-founder Douglas Chen, and several key R&D employees joined Google DeepMind to work on agentic coding technology. Google also took a non-exclusive license to some Windsurf technology.

July 14, 2025: Cognition, the company behind Devin — the first AI software engineer — announced it had acquired Windsurf. The deal included all intellectual property, product, trademark, brand, and business operations. Unlike the OpenAI deal, this acquisition closed quickly and cleanly.

April 2026: Windsurf 2.0 launched with built-in Devin integration, creating the first unified platform combining a local IDE agent with a cloud-based autonomous engineering agent.

Why OpenAI’s $3B Deal Fell Through

The collapse of OpenAI’s $3 billion acquisition of Windsurf was surprising given the size and strategic fit of the deal. Several factors contributed to the breakdown.

Regulatory scrutiny was the most commonly cited obstacle. At $3 billion, the acquisition would have been one of OpenAI’s largest and would have given the company a dominant position in both AI model development and AI-powered developer tools. Antitrust regulators, particularly in the United States and Europe, were already examining big tech’s acquisition patterns in AI. A deal that combined OpenAI’s foundational model strength with Windsurf’s developer tooling and enterprise customer base would have concentrated significant market power.

Strategic disagreements also played a role. OpenAI’s vision for Windsurf may have differed from what the Windsurf leadership wanted. Sources cited by The Verge suggested that integration plans and product direction became points of contention. Windsurf had built a strong brand and product identity, and its founders may have been unwilling to submerge that into OpenAI’s broader product roadmap.

Timing and market conditions added pressure. The AI coding tools market was moving fast. Cursor was gaining momentum, GitHub Copilot was integrating deeply with the Microsoft ecosystem, and new entrants were emerging. A prolonged regulatory review could have left Windsurf in limbo for months — a dangerous position in a market where product cycles are measured in weeks.

The collapse created an opening that both Google and Cognition were quick to exploit.

Google’s Talent Grab — A New Playbook for AI M&A

When the OpenAI deal fell through, Google moved with unusual speed. Rather than attempting to acquire Windsurf outright — which would have faced its own regulatory hurdles — Google targeted the company’s leadership and technical talent.

CEO Varun Mohan, co-founder Douglas Chen, and key R&D staff joined Google DeepMind to work on agentic coding technology. Google also secured a non-exclusive license to some Windsurf technology, giving it access to the product’s innovations without the regulatory baggage of a full acquisition.

This represents a new playbook for AI talent acquisition. Traditional M&A in tech has been about buying products, customer bases, and revenue streams. Google’s approach here was purely talent-driven. The company identified that the most valuable asset Windsurf possessed was not its code or its customers, but the expertise of its founding team in building agentic coding tools.

The strategy has precedents — Google’s acquisition of DeepMind itself was largely about talent — but applying it to a developer tools startup with $82 million in ARR is notable. It signals that the war for AI engineering talent has escalated to the point where companies are willing to pay premium prices for teams that have proven they can ship product in the AI coding space.

For Windsurf’s founders, the outcome was favorable. They received accelerated vesting and financial participation from the Cognition acquisition while also landing roles at one of the world’s premier AI research organizations.

Cognition’s Strategic Bet — Why Devin Needed Windsurf

Cognition’s acquisition of Windsurf was a strategic masterstroke that addressed several critical gaps in Devin’s market position.

Enterprise distribution was the most immediate need. Windsurf had 350+ enterprise customers and $82 million in annual recurring revenue, with enterprise ARR doubling quarter-over-quarter. Devin, despite its technical achievements as the first AI software engineer, had not yet built comparable enterprise sales momentum. Acquiring Windsurf gave Cognition instant access to a proven enterprise sales channel and a customer base that was already paying for AI coding tools.

Product complementarity was equally important. Devin is a cloud-based autonomous agent that can plan, implement, test, and deploy code independently. Windsurf is a local IDE that provides real-time coding assistance, planning, and prototyping. The two products are naturally complementary — Windsurf handles the fast, interactive development loop, while Devin handles the heavy lifting of autonomous implementation.

Brand and user base rounded out the picture. Windsurf had hundreds of thousands of daily active users and over 1 million total claimed users. This gave Cognition a massive installed base to cross-sell Devin to, and gave Windsurf users a path to more powerful autonomous capabilities.

The acquisition also eliminated a competitor. Windsurf and Devin were both competing in the agentic coding space. By acquiring Windsurf, Cognition consolidated the market and removed a rival that had strong enterprise traction and a growing user base.

The Numbers That Matter — $82M ARR and Enterprise Adoption

The financial metrics behind the Windsurf story tell a compelling story about the AI coding tools market.

Metric Value Source
OpenAI offer price $3 billion Bloomberg
Windsurf ARR at acquisition $82 million Cognition blog
Enterprise ARR growth Doubling quarter-over-quarter Cognition blog
Enterprise customers 350+ Cognition blog
Daily active users Hundreds of thousands Cognition blog
Total claimed users 1 million+ Substack analysis
Time from rebrand to acquisition ~5 months Multiple sources

The $82 million ARR figure is particularly significant. It validates that enterprises are willing to pay substantial sums for AI coding tools. Windsurf was not a free consumer product — it was a paid tool with real revenue, real customers, and real growth. The fact that enterprise ARR was doubling every quarter suggests that the market for AI-assisted development is still in its early stages and that adoption is accelerating.

The $3 billion offer from OpenAI, while it did not close, set a valuation benchmark for the AI coding tools space. At roughly 36x ARR, it reflected the market’s belief that AI coding tools represent a generational opportunity. For comparison, GitHub was acquired by Microsoft for $7.5 billion in 2018, and Copilot has since become one of Microsoft’s fastest-growing products.

The 350+ enterprise customers include companies across technology, finance, healthcare, and other sectors. This breadth of adoption suggests that AI coding tools are becoming infrastructure — not just a productivity boost for individual developers, but a strategic investment for engineering organizations.

What Windsurf 2.0 + Devin Means for Developers

The most tangible outcome of the acquisition for end users is Windsurf 2.0, launched in April 2026 with integrated Devin capabilities. The product combines two distinct modes of AI-assisted development.

The local agent (Windsurf IDE) handles planning, prototyping, and fast iterative development. It runs on the developer’s machine, provides real-time code suggestions, and helps with the day-to-day tasks of writing and refactoring code. This is the familiar Windsurf experience that hundreds of thousands of developers were already using.

The cloud agent (Devin) handles autonomous implementation, testing, and quality assurance. Developers can delegate complex tasks to Devin — implementing a feature end-to-end, writing tests, debugging issues — and monitor progress from within the Windsurf IDE. Devin runs in the cloud, so it can work on large-scale tasks without consuming local resources.

One-click delegation is the key workflow innovation. A developer working in Windsurf can identify a task that would benefit from autonomous execution — implementing a new API endpoint, refactoring a module, writing comprehensive tests — and delegate it to Devin with a single click. Devin takes over, plans the implementation, writes the code, runs tests, and presents the results for review.

The full loop — plan, delegate, monitor, review — happens within a single interface. This eliminates the context switching that previously required developers to move between tools or manually hand off work to teammates.

For individual developers, this means they can focus on the creative and architectural aspects of software development while delegating implementation work to the AI agent. For teams, it means faster delivery cycles and reduced bottlenecks.

The Bigger Picture — AI Coding Ecosystem Consolidation

The Windsurf saga is not an isolated event. It is part of a broader consolidation wave that is reshaping the AI coding tools market.

In early 2024, the market had at least five major players: GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf (then Codeium), Devin, and Amazon CodeWhisperer. Each had a different approach, different strengths, and different target audiences. The market was fragmented, and developers had to choose between tools that offered autocomplete, agentic capabilities, or full autonomous engineering.

By mid-2026, the landscape has consolidated dramatically:

  • Cursor has emerged as the leading standalone AI IDE, with strong adoption among individual developers and small teams.
  • GitHub Copilot has leveraged its integration with the Microsoft/GitHub ecosystem to maintain a dominant position in enterprise development.
  • Devin/Windsurf (Cognition) has created the first unified local+cloud agent platform, combining fast interactive coding with autonomous engineering.
  • Amazon Q Developer (formerly CodeWhisperer) has carved out a niche in the AWS ecosystem.
  • JetBrains AI and other IDE-native assistants continue to serve their respective ecosystems.

The consolidation reflects a market that is maturing rapidly. Early adopters experimented with multiple tools. The market is now entering a phase where platform-level integration, enterprise sales, and ecosystem lock-in are becoming the primary competitive differentiators.

The Three Remaining Powers — Cursor, Copilot, and Devin/Windsurf

The AI coding tools market is converging around three major platforms, each with a distinct strategic position.

Cursor has positioned itself as the developer’s choice. Its strength is in the quality of its code completion, its deep understanding of code context, and its focus on the individual developer experience. Cursor has built a loyal following among developers who want a fast, intelligent IDE that respects their workflow. Its challenge is scaling to enterprise customers who need compliance, security, and administrative controls.

GitHub Copilot benefits from the deepest ecosystem integration. It is built into GitHub, Visual Studio Code, and the broader Microsoft developer toolchain. For enterprises already using GitHub and Azure, Copilot is the natural choice. Its autocomplete capabilities have improved significantly, and its agentic features — Copilot Workspace, Copilot Chat — are expanding. The challenge for Copilot is that it is tied to Microsoft’s platform strategy, which may not appeal to developers who prefer independent tools.

Devin/Windsurf (Cognition) has the most ambitious vision: a unified platform that combines local IDE assistance with cloud-based autonomous engineering. The Windsurf acquisition gave Cognition the local IDE and enterprise distribution it needed. Devin provides the autonomous capabilities that no other tool fully matches. The combined platform is the only one that offers a complete loop from planning to autonomous implementation to review. The challenge is execution — integrating two products, maintaining both user bases, and delivering on the promise of seamless local-to-cloud development.

Capability Cursor GitHub Copilot Devin/Windsurf
Code autocomplete Excellent Excellent Good
Local IDE agent Yes Via VS Code Yes (Windsurf)
Cloud autonomous agent No Limited (Workspace) Yes (Devin)
Enterprise sales Developing Mature Mature (via Windsurf)
Ecosystem integration Independent Microsoft/GitHub Independent
One-click delegation No No Yes

What This Means for AI Coding Tool Users and Buyers

For developers and engineering leaders evaluating AI coding tools, the Windsurf sale has several practical implications.

The market is stabilizing. The period of rapid experimentation with dozens of AI coding tools is ending. The three major platforms — Cursor, Copilot, and Devin/Windsurf — are likely to dominate for the foreseeable future. Choosing a tool now means making a longer-term commitment to a platform and its ecosystem.

Enterprise buyers have more options. Windsurf’s $82 million ARR and 350+ enterprise customers prove that AI coding tools are enterprise-ready. The combined Devin/Windsurf platform offers a compelling value proposition for organizations that want both developer productivity tools and autonomous engineering capabilities.

The local vs. cloud debate is being resolved. Windsurf 2.0 + Devin shows that the future is not local OR cloud — it is both. The most powerful AI coding tools will combine fast local assistance for day-to-day development with cloud-based autonomous agents for complex, multi-step tasks.

Vendor risk has decreased. The Windsurf acquisition by Cognition, combined with Google’s talent investment, means that Windsurf’s technology and team are now backed by well-funded, committed organizations. Users of Windsurf can expect continued investment in the product.

Pricing pressure may increase. With three major platforms competing for the same customers, pricing is likely to remain competitive. The $3 billion valuation benchmark, however, suggests that the market sees significant room for growth, and prices may rise as tools add more autonomous capabilities.

Key Takeaways and Predictions for 2026-2027

The Windsurf sale is a defining event for the AI coding ecosystem. Here are the key takeaways and predictions for the next 12-18 months.

The talent acquisition playbook will spread. Google’s move to hire Windsurf’s founders and key engineers rather than buy the company will be replicated. As AI talent becomes the scarcest resource in technology, companies will increasingly pursue talent-only acquisitions, especially when full acquisitions face regulatory hurdles.

The local+cloud hybrid model will become the standard. Windsurf 2.0 + Devin has set a new benchmark. Within 18 months, every major AI coding tool will offer some form of local+cloud hybrid workflow. The standalone local IDE and the standalone cloud agent will both be seen as incomplete solutions.

Enterprise adoption will accelerate. The $82 million ARR figure and 350+ enterprise customers are early indicators. As AI coding tools prove their ROI in enterprise settings — faster delivery, reduced bugs, improved developer satisfaction — adoption will accelerate. Expect the total addressable market for AI coding tools to grow 3-5x by the end of 2027.

Regulatory scrutiny of AI acquisitions will increase. The failed OpenAI deal and Google’s talent grab both highlight the regulatory complexity of AI M&A. Expect more scrutiny of large AI acquisitions, more talent-only deals, and more creative deal structures designed to navigate regulatory constraints.

The line between AI coding tools and AI software engineers will blur. Windsurf 2.0 + Devin is the first product that combines interactive coding assistance with autonomous engineering. As these capabilities converge, the distinction between “AI coding tool” and “AI software engineer” will become increasingly artificial. The winners will be platforms that offer a seamless spectrum from autocomplete to full autonomy.

Consolidation will continue. The three major players — Cursor, Copilot, and Devin/Windsurf — will acquire or absorb smaller competitors. The market for standalone AI coding startups will shrink, and the barriers to entry will rise as incumbents build deeper integrations and stronger network effects.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did OpenAI’s $3 billion acquisition of Windsurf fall through?

The deal collapsed due to a combination of regulatory scrutiny and strategic disagreements. Antitrust regulators in the US and Europe were examining big tech’s AI acquisition patterns, and OpenAI’s vision for integrating Windsurf reportedly differed from what the Windsurf leadership wanted. The prolonged uncertainty created an opening that Google and Cognition quickly exploited.

What did Google get from the Windsurf situation?

Google hired Windsurf CEO Varun Mohan, co-founder Douglas Chen, and several key R&D employees to join Google DeepMind for agentic coding work. The company also secured a non-exclusive license to some Windsurf technology. This talent-focused approach gave Google access to proven AI coding expertise without the regulatory complications of a full acquisition.

How much revenue did Windsurf have when Cognition acquired it?

Windsurf had $82 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR) at the time of the Cognition acquisition. Enterprise ARR was doubling quarter-over-quarter, and the company had over 350 enterprise customers and hundreds of thousands of daily active users.

What is Windsurf 2.0 and how does it integrate Devin?

Windsurf 2.0, launched in April 2026, combines the Windsurf local IDE agent with Devin’s cloud-based autonomous engineering capabilities. Developers can plan and prototype locally in Windsurf, then delegate complex implementation tasks to Devin with one click. Devin handles the full implementation cycle — planning, coding, testing, and QA — and presents results for review within the Windsurf interface.

How does the Windsurf sale change the AI coding tools market?

The sale consolidates a fragmented market into three dominant players: Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and the combined Devin/Windsurf platform. It validates enterprise willingness to pay for AI coding tools, establishes the local+cloud hybrid model as the new standard, and signals that the era of standalone AI coding startups is giving way to platform-level competition backed by major strategic players.

item.title: Agentic IDE Architecture Deep Dive: How Cursor, Windsurf, and Antigravity Work Under the Hood
item.description: Explore the internal architecture of Cursor, Windsurf, and Google Antigravity — how their agent loops, context retrieval, and code application work under the hood.
item.content:encoded:
What Makes an IDE “Agentic”? — From AI-Assisted to Autonomous

An agentic IDE is a development environment where artificial intelligence does not merely suggest code completions but autonomously plans tasks, edits multiple files, runs terminal commands, debugs errors, and iterates until a goal is completed. Unlike traditional AI-assisted coding tools that require the developer to manage every step, agentic IDEs shift the developer’s role from “step-by-step operator” to “results supervisor.” The three leading platforms — Cursor, Windsurf (formerly Codeium, now part of Cognition), and Google Antigravity — each take a distinct architectural approach to achieving this autonomy, and understanding how they work under the hood reveals where the industry is heading.

The LLM-to-Agent Pipeline: How All Agentic IDEs Work Under the Hood

Every agentic IDE follows a three-phase evolution from basic completion to full autonomous agent. Understanding this pipeline is essential to appreciating the architectural differences between the platforms.

Phase 1: Basic Auto-Complete

The foundation of any AI coding tool is the language model’s ability to predict and suggest the next tokens a developer is likely to type. Cursor, Windsurf, and Antigravity all started with this capability. The model is trained on vast corpora of public code and fine-tuned to produce contextually relevant completions. At this stage, the IDE is purely reactive — it waits for the developer to type and offers inline suggestions. There is no planning, no multi-file awareness, and no tool execution.

Phase 2: Instruction-Tuned Chat

The second phase introduces a chat interface powered by an instruction-tuned model. Instead of merely completing the current line, the developer can ask the model to explain code, refactor a function, or suggest an implementation approach. Instruction tuning — where the base model is fine-tuned on pairs of human instructions and desired responses — enables the model to follow natural language commands. Cursor’s Composer, Windsurf’s Cascade chat, and Antigravity’s agent chat all operate at this level. The model can reason about code but still cannot execute changes autonomously.

Phase 3: Tool-Calling Agent Loop

The critical leap to “agentic” happens in Phase 3. The model is given access to tools — read file, write file, run terminal command, search codebase — and placed in a loop where it can plan, execute, observe results, and iterate. This is the agent loop, and it is the core architectural pattern shared by all three IDEs. The loop works as follows:

  1. Plan: The LLM receives a user request and generates a step-by-step plan using available tools.
  2. Execute: The model calls a tool (e.g., read_file to inspect a file, run_command to execute a build).
  3. Observe: The tool’s output is fed back into the model’s context.
  4. Iterate: The model decides whether the goal is met or another tool call is needed.
  5. Deliver: Once the goal is achieved, the model presents the result to the user.

The sophistication of this loop — how context is managed, how code is applied, how errors are handled — is where Cursor, Windsurf, and Antigravity diverge significantly.

Cursor: The Pioneer — Architecture Deep Dive

Cursor, valued at $29.3 billion as of November 2025 with backing from NVIDIA and Google, is the most mature agentic IDE on the market. It has been refining its agent architecture for over two years, and its internal design reveals the engineering that makes it the highest-scoring platform on SWE-bench at approximately 77%.

Context Retrieval: @-Tags and Vectorstore Indexing

Cursor employs a dual-strategy approach to context retrieval. The first strategy is explicit: developers use @-tag syntax to pull specific files (@file), folders (@folder), or documentation (@docs) into the model’s context. This gives the developer precise control over what the agent can see.

The second strategy is implicit: Cursor maintains a vectorstore index of the entire codebase. When the agent needs to find relevant code, it performs a semantic search against this index, retrieving the most relevant files based on embedding similarity. This vectorstore is built incrementally — as files change, their embeddings are updated in the background. The combination of explicit @-tagging and implicit vectorstore retrieval means Cursor can handle both developer-directed and autonomous context gathering.

The Apply Model: Semantic Diff → Linter Feedback → Self-Correction

One of Cursor’s most innovative architectural components is its multi-stage code application pipeline. When the agent decides to make a change, it does not simply write the new file content directly. Instead, it follows a three-stage process:

  1. Semantic Diff Generation: The LLM produces a semantic diff — a high-level description of what changed and why, rather than a raw text diff. This diff captures the intent behind the change.

  2. Apply Model: A separate, cheaper LLM (the “apply model”) receives the semantic diff and the original file and produces the actual modified file content. This separation of concerns means the expensive reasoning model focuses on planning while a cost-efficient model handles mechanical code generation.

  3. Linter Feedback and Self-Correction: After the apply model writes the changes, Cursor runs the linter on the modified file. If the linter reports errors, those errors are fed back into the agent loop, and the model iterates to fix them. Cursor enforces a three-iteration limit on this linter feedback loop to prevent infinite cycles.

This pipeline is remarkably efficient. According to developer reports, Cursor writes approximately 70% of code for power users, and the self-correction loop catches the majority of syntax and type errors before the developer ever sees them.

System Prompt Engineering: What Makes Cursor’s Agent Tick

Cursor’s system prompt is a carefully engineered artifact that shapes the agent’s behavior. Analysis of the prompt reveals several key design decisions:

  • XML Section Tags: The prompt uses XML-style tags to structure different sections (instructions, tools, constraints), making it easier for the model to parse and follow.
  • Explicit Model Identification: The prompt tells the model its own identity and capabilities, reducing hallucination about what it can and cannot do.
  • Anti-Apology Instructions: The prompt explicitly instructs the model not to apologize or over-explain — just produce the code. This reduces token waste and keeps the agent focused.
  • Tool-Only Code Output Enforcement: The model is instructed to output code exclusively through tool calls, never inline in chat responses. This ensures all changes are tracked and reviewable.
  • Three-Iteration Linter Loop Limit: The prompt caps the self-correction loop at three iterations, preventing the agent from getting stuck in infinite fix cycles.

Composer vs Agent Mode: When to Use Each

Cursor offers two distinct modes. Composer is a multi-file editing mode where the developer provides a prompt and Cursor generates changes across multiple files in a single shot. The developer reviews the diff and accepts or rejects. This is ideal for well-understood refactors where the developer wants to approve changes before they are applied.

Agent mode, by contrast, is fully autonomous. The agent plans, executes, runs tests, and iterates until the task is complete. The developer provides the goal and supervises the result. Agent mode is better for complex, multi-step tasks like implementing a new feature end-to-end, debugging a failing test suite, or setting up a CI pipeline.

Windsurf (Cognition): Enterprise-Grade Autonomy

Windsurf, originally built by Codeium, was acquired by Cognition (the company behind Devin AI) in July 2025. This acquisition brought Windsurf’s Cascade AI under Cognition’s enterprise umbrella, combining Windsurf’s developer-friendly interface with Devin’s autonomous SWE capabilities.

Cascade: Automatic Context Retrieval Without @-Tags

Windsurf’s Cascade is its most distinctive architectural feature. Unlike Cursor, which requires explicit @-tagging for precise context control, Cascade automatically retrieves relevant context from the codebase without any manual annotation. When a developer asks a question or issues a command, Cascade analyzes the query, performs semantic search across the codebase, and pulls in the files and symbols most likely to be relevant.

This auto-retrieval is powered by a combination of:

  • Code graph analysis: Cascade builds a dependency graph of the codebase, understanding imports, function calls, and type references.
  • Semantic embedding search: Similar to Cursor’s vectorstore, Cascade maintains embeddings of code symbols and files.
  • Relevance scoring: A lightweight model scores retrieved context by relevance to the current query, keeping only the most useful information within the token window.

The advantage of this approach is that developers can work with unfamiliar codebases without needing to know which files to @-tag. The disadvantage is less precise control — developers cannot force Cascade to look at a specific file if the auto-retrieval misses it.

Flow: Persistent Context Across Sessions

Windsurf’s Flow feature preserves context across development sessions. When a developer closes the IDE and returns later, Cascade remembers the project structure, recent changes, and ongoing tasks. This is achieved through a persistent context store that serializes the agent’s state — including file references, conversation history, and task progress — to disk. On session resume, the context is deserialized and injected into the model’s prompt.

This is particularly valuable for large projects where context windows are easily exhausted. Flow effectively gives Windsurf a form of long-term memory that Cursor and Antigravity currently lack.

Post-Cognition Acquisition: Devin AI Integration

The acquisition by Cognition in July 2025 has begun to bear fruit. Windsurf now integrates with Devin AI’s autonomous SWE capabilities, meaning that tasks too complex for a single Cascade session can be escalated to Devin’s multi-agent architecture. Devin handles the planning and execution of large-scale engineering tasks — creating PRs, running CI, deploying changes — while Windsurf handles the day-to-day coding within the IDE.

Enterprise Features: Admin Controls, Security, Compliance

Windsurf has the strongest enterprise offering of the three platforms. Post-acquisition, it offers:

  • Admin dashboards for managing team usage and permissions
  • SSO and SAML integration for enterprise identity management
  • Audit logging of all AI-generated code changes
  • Data residency controls for compliance with GDPR, SOC 2, and other frameworks
  • Custom model deployment for organizations that need to run models on their own infrastructure

These features make Windsurf the preferred choice for large organizations with strict compliance requirements.

Google Antigravity: Parallel Agent Orchestration

Antigravity, launched by Google on November 18, 2025, represents the most architecturally ambitious approach to agentic IDEs. Rather than a single agent loop, Antigravity orchestrates multiple agents running in parallel, coordinated by a central “Manager View.”

Manager View: Mission Control for 5 Parallel Agents

The Manager View is Antigravity’s signature feature. It is a dashboard that shows up to five agents working simultaneously, each in its own workspace. The developer can see each agent’s plan, current action, and output in real time. Agents can be assigned different tasks — one refactoring the backend, another updating the frontend, a third writing tests, a fourth running the build, and a fifth checking for security vulnerabilities.

This parallel architecture is fundamentally different from Cursor’s single-agent loop and Windsurf’s single Cascade session. It enables Antigravity to tackle large-scale refactors in a fraction of the time, but it also introduces coordination challenges that Cursor and Windsurf do not face.

Artifact-Based Communication: Plans, Screenshots, Task Lists

Antigravity uses artifacts as the communication layer between agents and between agents and the developer. When an agent creates a plan, that plan is saved as an artifact. When it takes a screenshot of a running application, that screenshot is an artifact. When it generates a task list, that too is an artifact.

These artifacts serve as both documentation and inter-agent communication. Agent A can reference Agent B’s plan artifact to understand dependencies. The developer can review artifacts to verify progress without reading every agent’s chat log. This artifact-based architecture is inspired by Google’s internal tooling and represents a novel approach to making multi-agent work transparent and auditable.

Chrome Integration: Browser Automation from the IDE

Antigravity is the only agentic IDE with built-in browser automation. Agents can launch Chrome, navigate to URLs, interact with web applications, take screenshots, and report visual results. This is particularly powerful for:

  • End-to-end testing: Agents can write code, deploy it, and verify the result in the browser.
  • Frontend development: Agents can see their changes rendered in real time.
  • API testing: Agents can interact with web UIs to verify API integrations.

The Chrome integration runs in a sandboxed environment, and all browser actions are recorded as artifacts for review.

Gemini 3 Pro’s 1M Token Context Window

Antigravity is powered by Google’s Gemini 3 Pro, which offers a 1 million token context window — roughly 10 times larger than typical GPT-4 or Claude deployments. This massive context window means Antigravity’s agents can hold an entire codebase in context simultaneously, eliminating the need for complex context retrieval strategies.

The practical implications are significant:

  • No need for @-tagging or vectorstore retrieval — the model can see everything.
  • Cross-file refactors are more reliable because the model can reason about all affected files at once.
  • Long-running agent sessions do not lose early context.

However, the 1M token context comes with higher latency and cost, which is why Antigravity is currently in free preview (with an expected price of approximately $20/month once it exits preview).

Head-to-Head Comparison: Architecture, Performance, and Pricing

SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench Scores

Platform SWE-bench Score Key Differentiator
Cursor ~77% Most mature agent loop, 2+ years of refinement
Antigravity 76.2% 1M token context, parallel agents
Windsurf ~75% Auto-context retrieval, enterprise features

All three platforms significantly outperform standalone models on SWE-bench, demonstrating the value of the agent loop architecture over raw model capability.

Context Retrieval Strategies Compared

Strategy Cursor Windsurf Antigravity
Explicit tagging @-tag syntax Not required Not required
Semantic search Vectorstore index Code graph + embeddings Not needed (1M context)
Auto-retrieval Limited Cascade auto-retrieval Full codebase in context
Cross-session memory No Flow feature No
Developer control High Medium Low (everything visible)

Agent Autonomy Spectrum: Full Delegation vs Inline Assistance

Cursor offers the widest spectrum of autonomy, from inline autocomplete (fully manual) through Composer (semi-autonomous) to Agent mode (fully autonomous). Windsurf sits primarily in the semi-to-fully autonomous range, with Cascade handling most context management automatically. Antigravity is designed for full delegation — the developer sets goals and supervises results, with the Manager View providing transparency into agent activity.

Pricing Tiers and Value Analysis

Platform Price Best For
Cursor Pro $20/month Individual developers and small teams wanting the most mature agent
Windsurf $15/month Enterprise teams needing compliance, audit, and admin features
Antigravity Free preview (~$20/month expected) Developers working on large codebases who want parallel execution

Windsurf offers the best value at $15/month, while Cursor commands a premium for its maturity and ecosystem. Antigravity’s free preview is the best deal currently available, but the expected $20/month price point puts it in line with Cursor.

How to Choose the Right Agentic IDE for Your Workflow

The right agentic IDE depends on your specific needs:

  • Choose Cursor if you want the most mature, battle-tested agent with fine-grained control over context and a proven track record on SWE-bench. It is ideal for developers who want to stay in the driver’s seat while leveraging AI for heavy lifting.

  • Choose Windsurf if you work in a large organization with compliance requirements, or if you frequently work with unfamiliar codebases where automatic context retrieval saves time. The Flow feature makes it particularly strong for long-running projects.

  • Choose Antigravity if you are tackling large-scale refactors that benefit from parallel agent execution, or if you want to experiment with the most innovative architecture on the market. The Chrome integration and 1M token context window are unique advantages.

All three platforms are VS Code forks, meaning your existing extensions, settings, and keybindings transfer seamlessly. There is no lock-in — you can switch between them as needed.

The Future of Agentic IDEs: Trends and Predictions

The agentic IDE market is evolving rapidly, and several trends are emerging:

  1. Multi-agent orchestration will become standard: Antigravity’s parallel agent architecture is likely to be copied by Cursor and Windsurf within the next 12-18 months. Single-agent loops are a bottleneck for large-scale tasks.

  2. Context management is the key differentiator: As models improve, the quality of context retrieval — not raw model capability — will determine which IDE performs best. Windsurf’s auto-retrieval and Antigravity’s massive context window represent two competing philosophies.

  3. Enterprise features will drive adoption: Windsurf’s post-Cognition enterprise push signals that the market is moving beyond individual developers. Admin controls, audit logs, and compliance certifications will become table stakes.

  4. Browser integration will expand: Antigravity’s Chrome integration points to a future where IDEs are not just for writing code but for verifying it end-to-end. Expect Cursor and Windsurf to add similar capabilities.

  5. Pricing will converge around $15-20/month: The current pricing range is narrow, and as features mature, the market will likely settle on a standard price point. The real competition will be on ecosystem, reliability, and developer experience.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between an AI-assisted IDE and an agentic IDE?

An AI-assisted IDE provides suggestions and completions that the developer must manually accept and apply. An agentic IDE autonomously plans, executes, debugs, and iterates on tasks — the developer supervises results rather than managing every step. The shift is from “tool that helps you code” to “agent that codes for you.”

Are Cursor, Windsurf, and Antigravity all built on VS Code?

Yes. All three platforms are forks of Microsoft’s Visual Studio Code. This means your existing VS Code extensions, themes, settings, and keyboard shortcuts work on all of them. The AI features are layered on top of the standard VS Code foundation.

Which agentic IDE has the best SWE-bench score?

Cursor leads with approximately 77% on SWE-bench, followed by Antigravity at 76.2% and Windsurf at approximately 75%. These scores are close and fluctuate with model updates, but all three significantly outperform standalone LLMs on software engineering tasks.

Does Antigravity require a Google account?

Yes, Antigravity is a Google product and requires a Google account to use. It runs on Google’s infrastructure and uses Gemini 3 Pro as its underlying model. The free preview is available to anyone with a Google account.

Can I use multiple agentic IDEs on the same project?

Yes. Since all three are VS Code forks, you can open the same project folder in any of them. Your files, git history, and node_modules are unaffected by which IDE you use. Many developers use Cursor for daily development and switch to Antigravity for large-scale refactors or Windsurf for enterprise compliance workflows.

item.description: A direct comparison of Cursor 3 and Google Antigravity in 2026 — covering SWE-bench scores, Agents Window vs Manager View, pricing, context windows, MCP...
item.content:encoded:
The AI IDE market in 2026 looks nothing like it did eighteen months ago. Cursor crossed $2 billion in annual recurring revenue in early 2026 — doubling that figure in just three months — and now commands 25% market share among generative AI software buyers. Then Google dropped Antigravity in November 2025: a free, agent-first IDE backed by Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.6, with benchmark scores that rival or exceed anything Cursor puts on the board. If you are evaluating which tool to standardize on — or deciding whether to keep paying for Cursor Pro — this comparison covers every dimension that matters: architecture, benchmark performance, pricing, security posture, and ecosystem depth.

Cursor 3 vs Google Antigravity 2026: The IDE Battle

The stakes in this comparison are unusually high. Cursor already has over 360,000 paying customers and is installed at more than 50% of Fortune 500 companies as of mid-2025 — including Nvidia, Uber, and Adobe — yet Google is entering the market with a fully free product that scores 76.2% on SWE-bench Verified. That combination of zero cost and top-tier benchmark performance is not something incumbents can ignore. Cursor responded with the April 2, 2026 release of Cursor 3, centered on the Agents Window — a standalone interface for managing multiple AI agents in parallel. Antigravity countered with a 2 million token context window, a five-agent Manager View, and the Artifacts system for verifiable agent action logs. The battle is no longer about autocomplete quality or single-file edits. It is about which platform gives a developer team the fastest path from idea to merged pull request when multiple agents are running simultaneously. Both tools have the architecture to support that workflow. The differences lie in maturity, ecosystem reach, and trust.

Cursor 3: What’s New in the $29B Valuation IDE

Cursor 3 launched April 2, 2026, and the headline feature is the Agents Window — a standalone interface for spawning and supervising multiple AI agents in parallel. Cursor crossed $2 billion in annual recurring revenue in early 2026, doubling in three months, which translates to a reported $29 billion valuation and 25% market share among generative AI software buyers. The Agents Window is not a cosmetic UI change. It replaces the single-session Composer model with a multi-agent orchestration layer where each agent gets an independent context, a dedicated diff view, and its own merge decision. Developers can spawn several agents against different branches or features simultaneously, monitor their progress in real time, review generated diffs side-by-side, and selectively merge results. Combined with Cursor’s existing MCP marketplace — which gives agents access to hundreds of plugins covering GitHub, Jira, Slack, databases, and more — the Agents Window enables end-to-end workflows where agents read an issue, write the fix, run tests, and open a pull request without developer intervention. Cursor’s SWE-bench score sits around 77%, supported by routing across Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, and GPT-4o depending on task complexity. For enterprise teams, Cursor carries SOC 2 Type II certification, GDPR compliance, SSO integration, and audit logging — the full compliance stack that regulated industries require before any tool touches production code.

Google Antigravity: The Free Agent-First IDE from Google

Google Antigravity landed in November 2025 as a Visual Studio Code fork, and its most disruptive feature is not technical — it is the price. Antigravity is completely free, and that includes access to Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.6 with no monthly fee. For context, Claude Opus 4.6 access through Cursor requires a paid plan. On the benchmark side, Antigravity scores 76.2% on SWE-bench Verified and 54.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, which measures autonomous multi-step terminal task execution including builds, test runs, and error recovery. The architecture centers on two modes: Editor View for standard coding, and Manager View for dispatching up to five parallel agents with real-time monitoring across a unified dashboard. The 2 million token context window is the spec that gets the most attention — it means an entire mid-size codebase can sit in context at once, bypassing the retrieval quality limitations of embedding-based search. The Artifacts system creates verifiable, immutable records of every agent action, which matters for compliance and post-incident debugging. Antigravity also supports third-party models including Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-OSS in a multi-model selection interface, along with native integrations for Google Cloud, Firebase, and BigQuery. The free pricing is a calculated land-grab: get developers inside the Google ecosystem, then monetize through Cloud spending. That strategy is coherent, but it also means Antigravity’s long-term roadmap is subordinate to Google’s broader platform priorities.

Benchmark Comparison: SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench, and Real Performance

SWE-bench Verified is the benchmark that matters most in 2026 for evaluating autonomous coding capability — it measures whether an AI can resolve real GitHub issues end-to-end without human guidance. Antigravity posts 76.2% on SWE-bench Verified; Cursor sits around 77% by reported figures. The gap is less than two percentage points, which means neither tool has a commanding lead on the primary industry benchmark. Where Antigravity adds unique data is Terminal-Bench 2.0, where it scores 54.2% — a benchmark specifically designed for multi-step autonomous terminal workflows including dependency installation, build execution, and iterative error correction. Cursor has not published Terminal-Bench results. For reference, in 2024 Devin scored 13.86% on SWE-bench and was considered a breakthrough. The entire category has moved from proof-of-concept to production-viable in roughly eighteen months. The practical implication of near-parity on SWE-bench is that benchmark scores should not be the deciding factor between these two tools. Both can handle the majority of well-scoped coding tasks autonomously. The differences that actually affect daily productivity are context management, tool integrations, and how cleanly the agent hands off work for human review. A developer running a medium-complexity feature branch will likely see similar output quality from either tool — what differs is the surrounding workflow infrastructure.

Benchmark Google Antigravity Cursor 3 Devin (2024)
SWE-bench Verified 76.2% ~77% 13.86%
Terminal-Bench 2.0 54.2% Not published —

Pricing: Free Antigravity vs $20/Month Cursor

Antigravity’s pricing is the most disruptive variable in this comparison. The tool is entirely free — Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.6 included, no usage caps published at launch. Cursor’s pricing runs in three tiers: a limited Free plan, a Pro plan at $20 per month that includes unlimited Composer 2 and agent mode with advanced model access, and an Ultra plan at $200 per month for maximum usage and priority support. Enterprise pricing is negotiated separately. The math for an individual developer is straightforward: Antigravity provides Claude Opus 4.6 access at zero cost, while Cursor Pro costs $20 per month for comparable model access. For a ten-person team, that is $200 per month in savings, or $2,400 per year. Google’s motivation is not altruism — the company is buying developer mindshare to drive Google Cloud consumption, and the unit economics work out if even a fraction of Antigravity users later deploy to Cloud Run or consume BigQuery. For enterprise procurement teams, however, the calculus changes. Free tools that lack SOC 2 certification, formal SLAs, and dedicated support channels create hidden costs — compliance reviews, security exceptions, and the risk exposure from deploying an uncertified tool on production codebases. Antigravity’s free pricing is compelling for individuals and early-stage teams; for regulated enterprises, the total cost of ownership calculation is more nuanced.

High-volume $200/month (Ultra) Not applicable
Included models Claude, GPT-4o routing Gemini 3.1 Pro + Claude Opus 4.6

Security and Enterprise Compliance: A Critical Difference

This section requires directness: Antigravity had five critical security vulnerabilities discovered within 24 hours of its November 2025 launch, including at least one remote code execution flaw. That is a significant signal about the maturity of the security review process behind the product. For any team running Antigravity on production code or within a corporate network, those vulnerabilities — and the response time to patch them — should be part of the risk evaluation. Cursor, by contrast, holds SOC 2 Type II certification, which means its security controls have been independently audited against the AICPA’s trust service criteria. That certification is not optional for most Fortune 500 procurement processes, which is part of why over 50% of Fortune 500 companies had adopted Cursor by mid-2025. Cursor also supports GDPR compliance, SSO integration via SAML, and audit log exports — the standard enterprise security stack. Antigravity has no published enterprise compliance certifications as of May 2026. The Artifacts system provides useful auditability at the agent action level, but that is not a substitute for platform-level security certifications. Google as a company has extensive security infrastructure, and it is reasonable to expect Antigravity’s certification posture will improve over time — but “will likely get there” is not a sufficient answer when a security team asks for documentation before approving a tool for production use. For teams in finance, healthcare, government contracting, or any environment with formal compliance requirements, Cursor is the only credible option between these two as of mid-2026.

MCP and Plugin Ecosystem: Cursor’s Marketplace vs Antigravity’s Limitations

Cursor’s MCP (Model Context Protocol) marketplace is one of its strongest competitive moats. With hundreds of plugins available — covering GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Linear, Slack, Notion, Figma, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and dozens of other services — Cursor agents can execute genuinely end-to-end workflows without leaving the IDE. A developer can configure an agent to read a Jira ticket, check out a branch, implement the fix, run the test suite via MCP, and open a GitHub pull request, all autonomously. That level of integration depth is not available anywhere else in the AI IDE market. Antigravity currently has no MCP support. Google has not announced a timeline for adding it. The tool instead leans on native integrations with Google’s own ecosystem: Google Cloud, Firebase, BigQuery, Google Workspace, and Cloud Run. For teams that are deeply committed to Google’s stack, those native integrations are genuinely useful — agents can read from BigQuery, deploy to Cloud Run, or update Firestore without any plugin configuration. But for the substantial majority of development teams that rely on GitHub, Jira, Slack, and non-Google databases, the absence of MCP support is a real constraint on what Antigravity agents can accomplish autonomously. Both tools support VS Code extensions since both are VS Code forks, which provides a baseline of compatibility for language servers, linters, and formatting tools. The meaningful ecosystem gap is at the agent integration layer — and there, Cursor’s MCP marketplace is not close to being matched.

Which IDE Should You Choose: Cursor 3 or Antigravity?

The answer depends entirely on your situation, and the honest framing is that these tools are not competing for the same primary use case right now. Antigravity is the right starting point for individual developers, small teams, and anyone working primarily within the Google Cloud ecosystem. You get Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro for free, a 2 million token context window that eliminates retrieval gaps on large codebases, and a clean five-agent parallel workflow through Manager View. The security vulnerabilities at launch are a concern, but for personal projects or pre-production work they are a manageable risk. Cursor 3 is the right choice for teams that need MCP integrations, enterprise compliance certifications, or a tool with a proven track record in regulated production environments. The Agents Window gives Cursor a credible multi-agent story, the MCP marketplace enables workflow automation that Antigravity cannot match, and SOC 2 Type II certification removes the compliance hurdle for enterprise procurement. The $20/month Pro cost is real, but it is not the deciding factor at the team level — the deciding factors are ecosystem reach and security posture. If you are currently paying for Cursor Pro and your team does not depend heavily on MCP integrations, it is worth running a 30-day parallel evaluation. Both tools perform similarly on SWE-bench, and the free Claude Opus 4.6 access in Antigravity represents genuine dollar savings at scale. But if your agents need to touch GitHub, Jira, Slack, or any non-Google external system autonomously, switching before Antigravity ships MCP support will cost you more in workflow reconfiguration than you save on subscription fees.

FAQ

Both Cursor 3 and Google Antigravity crossed 2026 with benchmark scores above 76% on SWE-bench Verified, which means the questions developers are asking have shifted from “can this thing code?” to “which one fits my team’s actual workflow?” The five questions below cover the decisions that come up most in practice: whether Cursor Pro is worth keeping, how to think about the context window difference, what the security vulnerabilities actually mean for your risk exposure, whether the tools can coexist on the same team, and what to watch for on MCP support in Antigravity. These are not edge cases — they are the exact tradeoffs that determine whether switching tools saves your team money or creates new friction. The short version: free beats paid for individual developers, MCP support keeps Cursor ahead for multi-system workflows, and compliance requirements make Cursor the only defensible option in regulated environments until Antigravity ships certifications.

Is Google Antigravity actually free, or are there hidden costs?

Antigravity is free to use including Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.6 access. Google has not published usage caps as of May 2026. The business model involves driving Google Cloud adoption rather than charging for IDE access directly. Hidden costs are indirect: teams that adopt Antigravity and build workflows around Google Cloud services will face switching costs if they later want to move to a different cloud provider.

Does Antigravity’s 2 million token context window make Cursor’s @codebase feature obsolete?

Not necessarily. The 2 million token window eliminates retrieval errors on large codebases by holding the entire codebase in context simultaneously. Cursor’s @codebase uses smart embedding search to select relevant files, which is more efficient for medium-size projects where the entire codebase does not need to be in context. For monorepos over 100,000 lines, Antigravity’s approach has a clear advantage. For typical mid-size projects, the practical difference is smaller than the headline spec suggests.

How serious were Antigravity’s launch security vulnerabilities?

Five critical vulnerabilities were found within 24 hours of launch, including a remote code execution flaw. That is a significant indicator of security testing maturity. Google patched the disclosed issues, but the discovery pattern suggests the pre-launch security review process was not comprehensive. Teams handling sensitive code or operating in regulated industries should treat Antigravity as insufficiently validated for production environments until it achieves formal compliance certifications.

Can Cursor and Antigravity be used together on the same team?

Yes, and some teams are doing exactly that. Cursor handles workflows that require MCP integrations and external tool access, while Antigravity handles tasks that benefit from the 2 million token context window. The tools use different underlying interfaces, so there is no direct sync between them, but there is no technical barrier to running both. The main cost is context switching overhead for developers who need to know both tools.

When will Antigravity add MCP support?

Google has not published a timeline for MCP support as of May 2026. Given that MCP is an open protocol originally developed by Anthropic and now widely adopted, it is reasonable to expect Antigravity will add support eventually. Until it does, any workflow that requires agents to interact with GitHub, Jira, Slack, or non-Google external systems will require Cursor or a different tool. This is the single most important capability gap to track if you are evaluating Antigravity for team adoption.

Three agentic IDEs now define how professional developers write code: Cursor, Windsurf, and Google Antigravity. SWE-bench scores sit within two percentage points of each other — Cursor at roughly 77%, Antigravity at 76.2%, Windsurf at roughly 75% — so raw benchmark numbers alone will not make this decision for you. The real differentiators are parallel agent architecture, security posture, and price-to-value ratio. This article works through each dimension so you can pick the right tool for your team without wading through marketing claims.

Cursor vs Windsurf vs Antigravity 2026: The Agentic IDE Market

The agentic IDE category did not exist in any meaningful form before 2023. By 2026 it commands serious enterprise budget and has triggered billion-dollar acquisitions. Cursor led the category into existence, shipping agentic features roughly two years before competitors matched them, and it shows in the numbers: 360,000+ paying customers and $2 billion in annual recurring revenue by early 2026. Windsurf survived a chaotic ownership saga — an aborted $3 billion OpenAI deal, a $2.4 billion Google talent acquisition of its founding team, and a $250 million Cognition buyout of remaining IP — yet still topped LogRocket’s AI Dev Tool Power Rankings in February 2026. Google Antigravity launched in late 2025 with a free preview that put parallel agent execution front and center, climbing immediately to second place in the same rankings. Stack Overflow’s 2025 survey found that 84% of developers use or plan to use AI coding tools and 51% do so daily, which explains why three well-funded products can coexist in the same market without cannibalizing each other entirely. The competition is healthy, the switching cost is low because all three share the same VS Code foundation, and the pressure is forcing rapid feature velocity across all three products.

Cursor: The Market Leader with $2B ARR and Agents Window

Cursor entered 2026 as the most mature agentic IDE on the market, and the financials back that up. With $2 billion in ARR, a $29.3 billion valuation from its November 2025 Series D, and more than half of Fortune 500 companies on its customer list, Cursor has enterprise credibility that neither Windsurf nor Antigravity can yet claim. The 360,000+ paying customers represent a signal that security teams have signed off, procurement has approved budgets, and the product survives real-world production workloads. On the technical side, Cursor’s Background Agents run in isolated cloud VMs — up to eight concurrently — so a misbehaving agent cannot touch your local file system. The proprietary SWE-1.5 model clocks 950 tokens per second, which the company claims is four times faster than comparable models in agent loops where code generation and test execution cycle repeatedly. Cursor also ships Design Mode with Figma integration, letting agents translate design specs into working components. SOC 2 Type II certification covers the compliance checkbox for most enterprise security policies. The weaknesses are real: Pro costs $20 per month and Business $40 per month, with heavy users potentially hitting $200 per month. A June 2025 price increase triggered visible community backlash and drove a measurable wave of migrations to Windsurf. The product is excellent, but you are paying a premium for category leadership and two years of compounded feature iteration.

Windsurf: Best Value at $15/Month with Cascade Context Engine

Windsurf delivers the most compelling value proposition in this comparison at $15 per month for Pro, $30 per month for Teams, and $60 per month for Enterprise — roughly 25 to 70 percent cheaper than Cursor depending on the tier. That price advantage is not accompanied by meaningful capability sacrifice. The Cascade context engine tracks every edit, command, and navigation action across a session, building a richer understanding of developer intent than simple file-based context. The Memories system persists project knowledge between sessions, so an agent that learned your codebase conventions on Monday still has that context on Friday. Wave 14 introduced Arena Mode, which lets two different AI models generate competing outputs for the same task and surfaces them side by side for blind comparison — a feature that has no equivalent in Cursor or Antigravity. The SWE-1.5 specialized model is built for software engineering tasks specifically rather than general-purpose language tasks. Perhaps most importantly for regulated industries, Windsurf holds both SOC 2 Type II and FedRAMP High certification, making it the only commercial agentic IDE cleared for U.S. federal government contracts and defense work. The Cascade RAG context engine handles million-line legacy codebases without the context loss that plagues simpler implementations. Despite three ownership changes in 2025 — ending with Cognition as the current steward — Wave 14 shipped on schedule and the February 2026 LogRocket ranking put Windsurf at number one. For most teams, especially those watching budget, Windsurf is the straightforward choice.

Google Antigravity: The Free Parallel Agent IDE with Security Caveats

Google Antigravity launched in late 2025 as the most architecturally ambitious of the three IDEs, and it is currently free in preview with a Pro plan expected around $20 per month when the preview ends. The defining feature is Manager View, which decomposes a high-level task into subtasks and runs up to five independent agents in parallel workspaces simultaneously, with a unified dashboard showing all five streams. Cursor and Windsurf run one agent at a time — Antigravity’s architecture is a genuine structural advantage for parallelizable work. The 2 million token context window dwarfs what the other two offer, and native Chrome integration means browser-based test automation works without additional configuration or separate tooling. The Artifacts system handles compliance documentation generation. SWE-bench at 76.2% is impressive for a product this new. However, the security record at launch was alarming: security researcher Aaron Portnoy disclosed five critical vulnerabilities — including remote code execution and data exfiltration — within 24 hours of the public release. A separate incident in December 2025 saw Turbo mode delete an entire developer D: drive without confirmation. Antigravity has no SOC 2 Type II, no FedRAMP High, and no published enterprise compliance roadmap. MCP support is also absent. For personal side projects in an isolated environment, the free preview is worth exploring. For any codebase that touches production systems or sensitive data, the security posture is not acceptable at this stage.

SWE-bench and Performance Benchmarks: How the IDEs Compare

SWE-bench measures an AI agent’s ability to resolve real GitHub issues autonomously, and it has become the de facto benchmark for agentic IDE comparisons because it tests the full loop: understanding a bug report, navigating a codebase, writing a fix, and validating that the fix passes tests. The 2026 standings are Cursor at approximately 77%, Antigravity at 76.2%, and Windsurf at approximately 75%. The two-percentage-point spread between first and last means that in roughly 1 in 50 tasks, one IDE succeeds where another fails — noticeable over thousands of tasks but not decisive for most daily work. Speed matters more than the top-line score in practice. Cursor’s SWE-1.5 model at 950 tokens per second means agent loops complete faster, and faster loops compound into real productivity differences across a full workday. Windsurf’s Cascade engine recovers context more reliably on large codebases, which matters when benchmarks on isolated repositories do not reflect the complexity of a real monorepo. Antigravity’s five parallel agents change the math entirely for workloads that decompose cleanly: if five agents each score 76.2% independently on separate subtasks, the probability that at least one produces a usable output is substantially higher than a single-agent run. The honest advice is to treat SWE-bench as a tiebreaker, not a primary filter. Run each IDE against your actual codebase on a representative task set for one week each before committing to a subscription upgrade or team migration.

The headline numbers favor Windsurf at every tier, but the total cost of ownership calculation depends on what you are buying. A 10-person engineering team on Cursor Business pays $4,800 per year. The same team on Windsurf Teams pays $3,600 per year — a $1,200 annual saving that funds roughly two months of additional Cursor seats if you ever want to run a parallel trial. Antigravity is free today, which makes it attractive for evaluation, but enterprise teams cannot make procurement decisions on a free preview with no published pricing, no SOC 2, and no support SLA. If FedRAMP High compliance is a hard requirement for your organization, the pricing comparison collapses — Windsurf is the only option regardless of price, making Cursor’s lower-tier advantage irrelevant. For everyone else, Windsurf’s pricing is the strongest argument in its favor when capabilities are this close.

Security and Enterprise Compliance: Who Can You Trust?
